To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the noise of a one-dimensional ballistic wire is quantized, that the quantized noise is sensitive to electron statistics, that the quantization is suppressed by electron degeneracy, that the quantal steps of conductance coincide with peaks of noise, that the noise of ballistic carriers is dominated by inelastic scattering in macroscopic leads, and that the noise of hot carriers depends, in a nontrivial way, on the inelastic energy loss in the leads.
the high-current ballistic fluctuations of one-dimensional conductors depend, directly and strongly, on carrier statistics, are observable, and are sensitive to inelastic scattering in the leads.
the noise of a one-dimensional ballistic wire is quantized, and the quantized steps coincide with the conductance steps.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the microscopic origin of current fluctuations in one-dimensional conductors and their connection with the quantization of conductance.
the microscopic theory of the classical-to-quantum crossover of ballistic fluctuations.
the quantum-classical crossover in the high-current transport of electrons in mesoscopic conductors, and with the fundamental role played by the nonequilibrium fluctuations of the current.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the high-current noise of ballistic wires is a robust, universal, and fundamental property of nonequilibrium quantum transport.
, contrary to widespread opinion and the Landauer- Buttiker paradigm, the high current noise of ballistic carriers is not an inessential detail but a fundamental feature of the quantum transport.
the Landauer-Büttiker model, while useful in many respects, is not sufficient to explain the observed quantization of conductance and its breakdown at higher currents.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the classical to quantum transition in one-dimensional ballistic conductors is a nonequilibrium phenomenon.
the quantum-classical crossover in ballistic transport is a nonequilibrium effect.
, in the quantum limit of one-dimensional wires, the conductance and noise are both determined by a single universal function of the carrier energy and the wire length.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in one-dimensional ballistic conductors, noise and conductance are not two distinct properties.
, in a one-dimensional ballistic conductor, the current noise is not only quantized but also strongly nonlinear, in a manner that is directly linked to the carrier statistics.
the conductance quantization of a single-mode wire is accompanied by the quantization of the noise.
